questions.prompt: Which best states the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)?

options.text: High-level modules should depend on low-level modules
High-level and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions; details depend on abstractions, not vice versa
You should use a dependency-injection container
Control should be inverted to the framework

questions.explanation: DIP is about the direction of dependencies: both high- and low-level code depend on abstractions. Using a container is DI/IoC tooling, not the principle.

questions.prompt: A web framework calls your route handler when a request arrives. Which idea is that primarily an example of?
questions.explanation: The framework controlling when your code runs ('don't call us, we'll call you') is Inversion of Control. It is not, by itself, DIP or DI.

questions.prompt: In DIP, the abstraction (interface) should be owned by the high-level ______, not by the low-level detail.
questions.explanation: The client/policy owns the interface it needs; the detail implements it, so the source-code dependency points inward.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its precise description.

pairs.right: A design principle: depend on abstractions, not concretions
A technique: supply a component's dependencies from outside
A broad idea: a framework/runtime controls the flow

questions.explanation: DIP is the goal, DI is a technique that helps reach it, and IoC is the wider family DI belongs to. They are related but not synonyms.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to invert a dependency from policy → detail into a compliant design.

items.text: Identify the volatile detail the policy calls
Declare an interface owned by the policy
Have the detail implement that interface
Inject the implementation at the composition root

questions.explanation: You define an interface the policy owns, implement it in the detail (flipping the source dependency inward), and supply the concrete via injection.

questions.prompt: Which statements are TRUE about DIP, DI, and IoC? Select all that apply.

options.text: DIP is a design principle about depending on abstractions rather than concretions
Dependency Injection is a technique for supplying a component's dependencies from outside
Using a DI/IoC container guarantees you are following DIP
You can follow DIP with no framework at all, just by passing arguments

questions.explanation: DIP is the principle, DI is a technique that helps achieve it, and both are distinct from IoC. A container only delivers objects — if inner code still imports concretions, DIP is violated regardless.
